reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it provides educational advice about uploading smartphone photos and videos for sale, including suitable subjects, technical limitations, and property-release conditions. Its earnings example is presented as a past result of about $450 over two and a half years, and the speaker says viewers should not expect to make tons of money. The affiliate links concern ordinary equipment purchases and are not described as required for the stock-photography opportunity.

citations.quote: so let me give you some advice on what I think smartphones are great for
So let's check which those are, and let's talk about some things that you have to take into consideration when shooting with your mobile phone.
you can definitely sell your phone photos and videos and make some money with them
One thing you need to remember here is that stock sites require property releases for that type of images.
I can't say that you will make tons of money with those but they will sell from time to time.

opening.argument: The video links a simple viewer activity to a monetary outcome: viewers are told they can sell mobile-phone photos on stock websites and make money. The speaker then supplies a concrete success story in which uploading three edited phone images allegedly produced around $450. That is a low-barrier income proposition built around taking ordinary phone photos, editing them, and uploading them, with no demonstrated qualification or investment required. The practical instruction therefore functions as a direct route from participation to cash, rather than merely abstract photography discussion.

citations.quote: Learn how you can sell your mobile phone photos to make money on stock photography websites.
then I edited three of them and upload them together with other images from that shoot. And actually those three images together brought me around $450 in two and a half years

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this education does not remove the solicitation. The opening admits that viewers are directed to upload and sell phone content for money, while the $450 story supplies a concrete incentive to act. Property-release language merely describes one obstacle; it does not negate the broader promise that ordinary phone images can generate income. The presence of conditions can make a pitch sound more credible without proving that the opportunity is presented fairly.

citations.quote: you can definitely sell your phone photos and videos and make some money with them
those three images together brought me around $450 in two and a half years

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted material does not establish a deceptive or guaranteed return. The example is explicitly limited to about $450 over two and a half years, and the advice says some images sell only from time to time. The activity is selling submitted creative work, not a free cash withdrawal or an unexplained reward. Property releases and technical limitations further show that success depends on permissions, subject matter, and image quality.

citations.quote: those three images together brought me around $450 in two and a half years
I can't say that you will make tons of money with those but they will sell from time to time
stock sites require property releases for that type of images

opening.argument: Several inducement signals reinforce one another. The video displays a $450 figure while recounting earnings from only three phone photos, and it says that finding a hot editorial topic could produce a nice income. It also sends viewers toward an email newsletter and includes numerous external affiliate purchase links. Although none of these facts alone proves misconduct, together they create a promotional pathway: attention is captured by a specific cash result, urgency is suggested by hot topics, and outside links provide actions around the money-making message. The careful judge should treat the attractive return framing as materially stronger than the disclaimers.

citations.quote: And if you find the hot topic here I think you can make a nice income from those
Subscribe to my email newsletter: https://lukaazman.ck.page/63e38f1c2f
Some links in my video description are affiliate links, that means I will make a small commission if you click them and make a qualifying purchase

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense emphasizes caveats but underplays the combination of signals. A disclosed affiliate arrangement still monetizes clicks and purchases, while the $450 figure and hot-topic income language make the opportunity attractive. Saying the amount took two and a half years does not eliminate the effect of displaying a large round-dollar result alongside instructions to upload content. The cautions can operate as credibility-building details within a broader promotional message.

citations.quote: Some links in my video description are affiliate links, that means I will make a small commission if you click them and make a qualifying purchase
And if you find the hot topic here I think you can make a nice income from those

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The evidence does not show urgency, guaranteed earnings, or a required purchase. The $450 example is a past result over two and a half years, while the speaker expressly says he cannot promise large earnings. “Hot topic” is a conditional discussion of editorial demand, not an instruction to pay or deposit money. The description identifies the links as affiliate links for ordinary purchases and says the commission is small, which is not evidence that viewers must buy anything to earn.

citations.quote: those three images together brought me around $450 in two and a half years
I can't say that you will make tons of money with those but they will sell from time to time
Some links in my video description are affiliate links, that means I will make a small commission if you click them and make a qualifying purchase

opening.argument: The instructional format functions as promotion for participation in an income opportunity. The title asks whether viewers can earn money selling phone photos, the description promises to explain how to sell them for money, and the speaker closes by urging viewers to subscribe for more stock-photography material. The video does not simply analyze photography; it steers viewers toward uploading images, finding commercially useful events, and following the creator's continuing funnel. Advice about camera limitations makes the pitch appear balanced, but the central behavioral message remains: use a phone, submit content, and pursue earnings.

citations.quote: Can you EARN MONEY selling PHONE PHOTOS? | Stock photography tips and tricks
Learn how you can sell your mobile phone photos to make money on stock photography websites.
you can definitely sell your phone photos and videos and make some money with them
if you want to learn more subscribe to my channel and also hit the bell

rebuttal.rebuttal: The label “tutorial” does not settle how the content operates. The title foregrounds earning money, the description directs viewers to a newsletter and other links, and the closing subscription request extends the creator's commercial funnel. Technical warnings may make the presentation seem trustworthy, but they also help overcome skepticism about using a phone. The relevant question is whether the overall framing drives participation, and these calls to action show that it does.

citations.quote: Can you EARN MONEY selling PHONE PHOTOS? | Stock photography tips and tricks
Subscribe to my email newsletter: https://lukaazman.ck.page/63e38f1c2f
if you want to learn more subscribe to my channel and also hit the bell

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Those calls to action promote the creator's educational channel and newsletter, not a payment scheme. The content also tells viewers what phone photography is poor at: low light, dynamic range, depth of field, and lens choice. It expressly limits the earnings discussion by saying images may sell only from time to time. A request to subscribe or receive a newsletter does not establish that viewers are promised cash for a simple action or required to purchase access.
